stackAndServices: TypeScript/React on Remix (post-Next.js migration) frontend with a Konva canvas editor; Node/tRPC-style backend; single Postgres via Prisma ORM (`Field`, `Envelope`, `EnvelopeItem`, `Recipient` tables). Single-repo monolith; this claim involves no cross-service egress.
compiledPromise: Discriminating claim: in the envelope field editor, Shift+click on a field ADDS it to (or, if already selected, REMOVES it from) the current multi-selection without discarding the rest of the selection; a plain click (no Shift) collapses the selection to just the clicked field. Deleting the active multi-selection via the toolbar's Remove action deletes exactly the shift-selected fields' rows from the `Field` table for that envelope, leaves un-selected fields' rows intact, and a fresh load of the editor (or fresh session) shows only the surviving field(s). Negative: the un-selected field must NOT be deleted, and fields removed from the selection via a second Shift+click (toggle-off) must NOT still be deletable as part of the group.
conjureFeasibility: Real, not doubled. Documenso is self-hostable end-to-end (Remix app + Postgres via Prisma) and the repo already wires a Playwright harness against a live app + live DB (packages/app-tests) — evidence I used only to judge conjure-feasibility, not as review/CI signal for the verdict. No egress/webhook effect is in scope for this claim, so the sealed-room/egress-ledger machinery isn't needed at all — this is close to the cleanest possible P' shape: pure persisted-state delta on one clean relational table (`Field`), dual-leg satisfiable via (i) harness DB diff on `envelope.fields` and (ii) a fresh navigation back into the "addFields" step of the same editor.
verdictBasis: Predicted from static reading of the diff + surrounding system code only (I did not actually execute a harness — no build, no browser drive, no DB diff was captured; see confession). The diff removes a stage-level 'click tap' handler that computed shift/ctrl/meta multi-select logic by reading `transformer.nodes()` AFTER the click had already bubbled up from a field-group handler that unconditionally reset selection to one node — a stale-read race that likely made old shift-click behavior unreliable. The new code puts all multi-select logic directly in the field-group's own click handler, reading `interactiveTransformer.current.nodes()` (an imperative Konva ref updated synchronously inside `setSelectedFields`, not the batched React state) before computing the toggle — this removes the race. Deletion (`deletedSelectedFields`) reads from `selectedKonvaFieldGroups`, the React state that `setSelectedFields` populates, so as long as the click handler calls `setSelectedFields` with the correct node list (which the new logic does), delete acts on exactly the shift-selected set. `Field` is a flat table keyed by `envelopeId` with no denormalization, so an effect check ("3 fields -> delete 2 shift-selected -> 1 remains, correct one survives") binds cleanly to an observed DB delta. Confession: this is a code-reading judgment, not an executed-and-sealed verdict — under strict P' (NOT-EXECUTED -> CND) the honest procedural answer for "has this actually been verified today" is CND; WORKS here is my prediction of what a real run would show, which the exercise's blind protocol treats as the deliverable. notCovered: cross-page shift-selection (each page appears to be its own component instance with its own transformer ref/state, so shift-click across two different PDF pages may not merge into one selection — not addressed by the diff or its tests); touch/mobile input (no Shift key equivalent); interaction between marquee-drag selection and shift-click on the same selection (PR narration claims they "complement" each other but no test exercises the combination).
holds: Front-door walk (P'.a) is a clean fit: the whole claim is driven purely by click/shift-click/navigate on the editor canvas, no forging needed.

Dual-leg effect check (P'.b) is unusually clean here: one flat DB table (Field) keyed by envelopeId, no async/egress, so both legs (harness DB diff + fresh-session re-navigation into the editor) are trivial to wire without touching the egress/sealed-room machinery at all.

Mutation-attribution calibration (1.2) is easy: the only relevant write path is the delete-fields mutation scoped to one envelope under test; no idle-baseline noise concern in a single-tenant test fixture.

Reproduce-to-convict / k-of-N (P'.d) is straightforward: the flow is fully deterministic given fixed click coordinates and a unique externalId per run, so re-running from a fresh world N times is cheap.
No egress effect in scope, so FW-12/FW-14-style fixture-world and sandbox-config divergence risks are minimal for this particular claim.

breaks.detail: The effect check's front-door steps depend on exact pixel coordinates landing on the right Konva shape inside a <canvas>, which is more brittle than DOM selectors (PDF viewport scaling, zoom, font metrics can shift hit-boxes). A generic 'click/type/navigate' driver vocabulary (1.2) may not have a canvas-aware hit-test primitive, which would manifest as spurious CNDs (misclick opens the floating toolbar or hits the wrong field) that have nothing to do with feature correctness.
breaks.fix: Give the read-only cross-exam driver a canvas-aware locate-and-click primitive (e.g. resolve field bounding boxes from the app's own Konva node registry rather than raw pixel coordinates) before trusting CND-vs-WORKS distinctions on canvas UIs.

breaks.detail: The claim's happy-path sequence (click, shift+click add, shift+click remove, shift+click re-add) is the only order exercised. A hostile prober reordering these (e.g., shift+click first with nothing selected, or two rapid shift+clicks on the same field) could expose races between the synchronous transformer.nodes() read and the deferred editorFields.setSelectedField state update that the happy path never surfaces.
breaks.fix: Require at least one adversarial click-ordering variant in the hostile-class set for any claim about toggle/stateful UI selection, not just the intended sequence.

breaks.detail: The PR's own comment says shift+click 'complements' marquee-drag multi-select, implying an interaction surface (drag a marquee, then shift+click to remove one member) that neither the diff's tests nor my compiled claim cover.
breaks.fix: Either add a second discriminating claim for marquee+shift interplay, or explicitly record it as notCovered so a WORKS on the narrow claim isn't read as a WORKS on 'multi-select' broadly.

newVectors: FW-15 (proposed): 'prediction-without-receipts' — a verdict authored by reasoning over diff+schema alone can read as confident WORKS prose with zero actual receipts behind it; this is a variant of FW-2 pointed inward at the verdict-authoring step itself, not just the harness. CND-by-default must be enforced by checking for a receipts pointer, not by trusting narrative confidence.

Canvas/non-DOM front-door boundary — for features whose front door is a <canvas> (Konva, WebGL, etc.) rather than DOM elements, structural CND rate may be higher than for DOM UI for reasons orthogonal to correctness (coordinate drift, hit-testing gaps in the driver), which could bias any cross-feature WORKS/CND comparison that doesn't control for front-door modality.
sonnetDifficulty: The hard part for me was not the feature's surface behavior (that's simple) but reconstructing the OLD code's actual runtime behavior well enough to judge whether this PR is a genuine bug fix or a no-op refactor. That required mentally simulating Konva's event-bubbling order (field-group click handler fires before the bubbled stage-level handler) crossed with React's state-update batching (the stage handler's `transformer.nodes()` read could see a stale selection because the field-group handler's `setSelectedFields` call hadn't flushed yet) — a subtle async-ordering judgment that's easy to skip past and just trust the PR's own comment ('the new behaviour'). A shallower pass would have taken that narration at face value instead of independently deriving why the old path was broken. Separately, and more materially to this exercise's honesty requirement: I had no way to actually stand up Documenso (Postgres + Remix dev server + Playwright) in this sandbox within budget, so the entire verdict is a code-reading prediction rather than a sealed-receipts result — that gap is exactly the FW-15 vector I flagged, and I want to be explicit that a real P' pipeline run is the only thing that would upgrade this from 'plausible' to a defensible WORKS.
